Some Remarks on Tensor Rank

2-tensors

Definition 1 (Simple tensor) Say x∈V1⊗⋯⊗Vn is simple, whenever x=v1⊗⋯⊗vn for some vi∈Vi.

Definition 2 (Rank of a tensor) The rank of x∈V1⊗⋯⊗Vn is the least number r such that x is the sum of r simple tensors.

  • By definition, rank(0)=0​​.

Proposition 1 One has the following propositions.

  1. If ∑i=1rui⊗vi=0 and {ui}i=1r is a linearly independent set, then vi=0 for each i​.

  2. Let W be a subspace of V. We identify U⊗W as a subset of U⊗V via id⊗(W↪V). For any x∈U⊗W⊂U⊗V such that x=∑i=1sui⊗vi, if {ui}i=1s are linearly independent, then span(vi)⊂W.

Proposition 2 Features of U⊗V for arbitrary vector spaces U and V.

  • (Invariance under field extensions) rank(−) is invariant under field extensions,

  • (Sub-additivity) rank(x+y)≤rank(x)+rank(y),

  • (Homogeneity) rank(λx)=rank(x) for λ≠0,

  • Set r=rank(x). Whenever x=∑i=1rui⊗vi is a minimal decomposition, span({ui}i=1r) is an r-dimensional subspace of U, which is unique with respect to the choice of x=∑i=1rui⊗vi​.

Proposition 3 If U and V are finite dimensional, then U⊗V≅L(U∗,V)≅kdim⁡U×dim⁡V.

Proof The linear isomorphism is given by

(1)U⊗V→L(U∗,V),u⊗v↦[f↦f(u)⋅v].

By dual basis, u⊗v∈U⊗V identifies u⋅vT (a rank-1​​​ matrix).

Proposition 4 Let k be a number field. One can take k=R or C for an easy exploration to the following properties. By identification of U⊗V and km×n, one has the followings.

  • (The probability for finding a tensor with given rank) Suppose that m≤n. Then {x∣rank(x)<m} is a closed set with empty interior, where as {x∣rank(x)=m}​ is a dense open set.

  • (Zariski topology, definability) For any r, the set {x∣rank(x)=r}​ is determined by a finite set of polynomials.

Multi-tensors over real or complex fields

Definition 1 For x∈V1⊗⋯⊗Vn, and y∈U1⊗⋯⊗Um​, one defines

(2)x⊗y∈V1⊗⋯⊗Vn⊗U1⊗⋯⊗Um.

Notion 1 Write x⊗2=x⊗x, and x⊗(n+1)=x⊗n⊗x.

Proposition 5 The following properties holds.

  • (Homogeneity) rank(λx)=rank(x) for λ≠0;

  • (Invariance under the extension of subspaces) Let ik:Vk↪Wk be injection, then rank(x)=rank((i1⊗⋯⊗in)(x));

  • (Sub-additivity) rank(x+y)≤rank(x)+rank(y)​​.

  • The maximal possible rank is also sub-additive, that is, for vector spaces with finite dimensional:

    (3)max(rank(U1⊗U2))≤max(rank(U1))⋅max(rank(U2)).

Proposition 6 The following equalities no longer hold in general.

  • (Sub-multiplicity) rank(x⊗y)≤rank(x)⋅rank(y);

  • (Monotony under field extensions) Let F↪E be any field extension. Then rankF(x)≥rankE(x).

  • Let V:=V1⊗⋯⊗Vn be a multi-tensor space. For r, the set {x∈V∣rank(x)=r}​ can be neither open nor closed, even undetermined by finite many polynomials.

  • There exists r1≠r2 such that each {x∈V∣rank(x)=ri} contains some open balls, for i=1,2​.

Proposition 7 Let {ei}i=1n⊂V be linearly independent, then x=∑i=1rei⊗n∈V⊗n has rank r​.

Proof (Rank ≤r) Clear.

(Rank ≥r) Without the loss of generality, let V be finite dimensional, as the tensor rank is invariant under the expansion of subspaces. Take f∈V∗ which sends every ei to 1. Since (f⊗n−1⊗id)(x) has rank r, the tensor x has rank ≥r.

Example 1 Let x=(10) and y=(01) be the standard basis of k2. Now consider

(4)τ:=x⊗x⊗y+x⊗y⊗x+y⊗x⊗x−y⊗y⊗y∈k2⊗k2⊗k2.

Suppose that k=R, then rank(τ)=3. The proof is as follows.

  • (Rank ≤3) Consider θ1=(x+y)⊗3, θ2=(x−y)⊗3, and θ3=y⊗3. Hence, τ=12(θ1−θ2)−2θ3.

  • (Rank ≠2) Suppose that τ∈R2⊗span(u1⊗v1,u2⊗v2). Since

    (5)τ=x⊗(x⊗y+y⊗x)+y⊗(x⊗x−y⊗y),

    and {x,y} is linearly independent, we learn from Proposition 2 that

    (6)(x⊗x−y⊗y),(x⊗y+y⊗x)∈span(u1⊗v1,u2⊗v2).

    Suppose that a(x⊗x−y⊗y)+b(x⊗y+y⊗x) is simple, one has

    (7)0=det(abb−a)=a2+b2.

    Hence a,b=0, a contradiction.

Suppose that k=C, then rank(τ)=2. The proof is as follows:

  • (Rank ≤2) Consider a=1 and b=i in the previous proof. One has

    (8)(y+ix)⊗3+(y−ix)⊗3=−2τ.

  • (Rank ≥2) Consider f:C2→C determined by x↦0 and y↦1. Then

    (9)(f⊗id⊗id)(τ)=x⊗x−y⊗y.

    Since x⊗x−y⊗y has rank 2, τ has rank ≥2.

Example 2 In previous example, one defines the symmetric tensor τ0=x⊗x⊗x, τ1=∑cycx⊗x⊗y, τ2=∑cycx⊗y⊗y, and τ3=y⊗y⊗y. One learns from binomial extension that

(10)τ0+λτ1+λ2τ2+λ3τ3=(x+λy)⊗3.

Consider the tensor θ(t):=τ1+tτ2+t2τ3.

  1. If t≠0, then θ(t)=1t((x+ty)⊗3−x⊗3) has rank 2 (rank ≠1 is clear).

  2. If t=0, then θ(t)=τ1 has rank 3. To see that rank ≠2​, use the test in example 1.

Hence, the space of rank 2 tensors is never defined via the zero sets of finite many polynomials.

Example 3 We shall prove that (over C) rank(τ1⊗τ1)<9=rank(τ1)3. Consider

(11)τ1⊗τ1=(τ1+τ3)⊗(τ1+τ3)−(τ1+τ3/2)⊗τ3−τ3⊗(τ1+τ3/2).

Hence, rank(τ1⊗τ1)≤2×2+2+2=8.

Example 4 Classification of tensors over k2⊗k2⊗k2.

  • (Construction by Y. Zhao) First, there is no tensor of rank 4. It suffices to prove that every tensor of the form

    (12)τ=u1⊗x⊗x+u2⊗x⊗y+u3⊗y⊗x+u4⊗y⊗y

    reduces to the some of 3 simple tensors. Without the loss of generality,consider

    • (Case I) u2=λ1u1+λ2u3​. Then

      (13)τ=u1⊗x⊗(x+λ1)+u3⊗y⊗x+u4⊗(λ2x+y)⊗y.

    • (Case II) u1=k1u4, and u2=k2u3. Then

      (14)u4⊗(k1x⊗x+y⊗y)+u3⊗(k2x⊗y+y⊗x).

      As one divide k1x⊗x=(k1−k2)x⊗x+k2x⊗x, the rest is clear.

  • Say x and y are equivalent, whenever there is φi∈Gl2(k) such that (φ1⊗φ2⊗φ3)(x)=y​. For algebraically closed fields, one can prove the equivalence classes are exactly

    (15)[0],[τ0],[x⊗(x⊗2+y⊗2)],[x⊗3+y⊗x⊗x],[(x⊗2+y⊗2)⊗x],[τ0+τ3],[τ1].

    Hence, rank 1 tensors are equivalent to τ0, while rank 3 tensors are equivalent to τ1.

Example 5 This example focus on an interesting problem:

  • when we randomly select a tensor x∈k2⊗k2⊗k2 (k=R or C), what is the expectation of rank(x)?

The probability should be compatible with the topology of Euclidean spaces. At least, for any F⊂kn with empty interior, the probability of the event {x∈F∣x∈Rn} must be 0. By assumption, a randomly selected X∈kn×n has probability 1​​ to be invertible.

However, if one identify (k2)⊗3 as k2×2×2, the space of cubes (matrices in 3-dimension), and consider the independent normal distribution N(0,1) for each (ai,j,k)1≤i,j,k≤2, the distribution are as follows.

  • The analysis of k=C is easy. One can prove that the orbit of τ0 under the action of Gl2(C)⊗3 contains in the orbit under C2×2⊗GL2(C)⊗2, while the orbit of x⊗x∈C2⊗C2 under GL2(C)⊗2 coincides the closed subset of rank 1-matrices, which has empty interior. The analysis for rank 3​ tensors is similar.

  • The analysis of k=R requires the following lemma: let θk=(ai,j,k)∈R2×2 (k=1,2) be the slices of the tensor θ∈R2×2×2, the following proposition holds with probability 1:

    • rank(θ)=2 whenever det(λθ1+θ2)=0 has 2​ real solutions.

      1. (⇒) Let θ=∑l=1,2ul⊗vl⊗wl. Then

        (16)θl=(u1u2)⋅((w1)l(w2)l)⋅(v1v2)T(l=1,2).

        One notices that both (u1u2) and (v1v2) has probability 1 to be invertible. Hence, det(λθ1−θ2) has probability 1 to have real 2 roots.

      2. (⇐) One only needs to find u, v and w's. Consider

        (17)(λθ1−θ2)≃θ1−1(λI−θ1−1θ)≃θ1−1(λI−PΛP−1)≃(θ1−1P⋅λI⋅P−1−θ1−1P⋅Λ⋅P−1).

        where ≃ means to have probability 1 to be equal.

      The probability of det(λθ1+λ2) to have 2 real eigenvalue is π/4 (Link).

Example 6 (Computational complexity) How many operations of multiplications are required in order to multiply 2×2 matrices? The answer is 7​, which is proved to the best answer (History of Strassen Algorithm).

Now we consider the tensor form of matrix multiplication, which is the bilinear form

(18)(−×−):k2×2,k2×2→k2×2.

Such multiplication is a tensor in (k2×2⊗k2×2)∗⊗k2×2≅(k2×2)⊗3, which writes

(19)∑1≤i,j,k≤2Ei,j⊗Ej,k⊗Ei,k.

By first paragraph in the introduction part of this article, one has

(20)(−×−)Linear Operators⟷Fewest multiplicationsStrassen’s lemma↓↓↓↓V∗⊗V∗⊗VTensor Forms⟷Rank of the tensor7.

Hence, rank(∑1≤i,j,k≤2Ei,j⊗Ej,k⊗Ei,k)=7, which is independent of the choice of fields. When considering the block matrices, one has

(21)rank(∑1≤i,j,k≤nEi,j⊗Ej,k⊗Ei,k)≤C0⋅nlog2⁡7.
